clue.text: In this sort of voting, job often involves delivery

parts.note: a post is a job or position

indicators.note: involves means the word for often wraps round the word for delivery

parts.note: a lot means often, frequently
in cricket a delivery is a ball bowled

explanation.surface: A remark on a kind of election in which the work mostly means handing things over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivery' suggests the postman's round, but it is a cricket term: a ball bowled to the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of vote is cast by mail rather than in person at a polling station.

clue.text: Fish appearing in dock reversed shortage

indicators.note: reversed means the word for dock is turned round

parts.note: to dock is to cut off, lop
a lack is a shortage

explanation.surface: A fish appears in a dock after a shortage turned around.
explanation.definitionFit: Pollack is a food fish of the cod family found in the North Atlantic.

clue.text: Son with slight temperature avoids food colouring

indicators.note: avoids means the letter for temperature is kept out of the word for slight

parts.note: a slight is an insult, an affront

explanation.surface: A boy running a mild fever turns down food dye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slight temperature' reads as a mild fever, but 'slight' is the noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Saffron, from crocus stigmas, is used as a yellow dye for rice and baking.

clue.text: Tensions exist in a European novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Tensions are present in a book by a European writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book, but it is the adjective meaning new.
explanation.definitionFit: Worries and nervous strains are tensions, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Overenthusiastically toasted end of graduation in Lancaster?

indicators.note: in means the final letter goes inside the actor's first name

parts.note: Burt Lancaster was an American film actor

indicators.note: end of points to the final letter of the word graduation

explanation.surface: Cheering a graduation at Lancaster University a little too keenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lancaster' suggests the university town, but it is the Hollywood star Burt Lancaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Toast left too long under the grill is charred, so overdone toasting gives this adjective.

clue.text: Cut grey lining in case where pins are laid

indicators.note: lining means the shortened colour lines the inside of the word for in case

parts.note: lest means in case, for fear that

indicators.note: cut means the word grey loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Cut grey cloth lines a case for storing pins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pins' looks like sewing pins, but it is slang for legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pins is informal for legs, and a footstool-like support is where they rest.

clue.text: Regularly used coercion, force, on foreign banker

indicators.note: regularly used means every other letter of the words that follow is taken

explanation.surface: Coercion and force are applied habitually to a foreign financier.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of 'coercion force on' make the answer; 'banker' is crossword slang for a river, something with banks.
explanation.definitionFit: A banker is a river in crosswords, and the Orinoco flows through Venezuela and Colombia, so it is foreign.

clue.text: Polish GP isn't, unfortunately, everything you'd wish for

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Sadly, the Polish family doctor is not everything you'd want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like the nationality, but its letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A list of the items you want to buy on a trip to the shops is, playfully, all you wish for.

clue.text: One housed in semi: feller in US town

indicators.note: housed in means the first piece is lodged inside the word for semi

parts.note: semi- means half
one is I, the Roman numeral
a feller is a tool that fells trees, an axe, spelt ax in American English

explanation.surface: A man living in a semi-detached house is a lumberjack in an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feller' looks like 'fellow', but it is a tree-feller, and 'in US' gives the American spelling AX.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a West Yorkshire town (and also the name of towns in Nova Scotia and the US).

clue.text: Description of playful Sir Hugo?

indicators.note: playful suggests the letters of the name frolic about into a new order

explanation.surface: A query about how to describe a mischievous knight called Sir Hugo.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of SIR HUGO, rearranged as 'playful' signals, make the answer, and the whole clue also defines it: a playful Sir Hugo would be described as mischievous.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischievous and impish in a playful way is exactly what this adjective describes, fitting a playful knight.

clue.text: Asserts much more than control

parts.note: to hold is to assert or maintain an opinion
way is informal for much, as in way better
over means more than

explanation.surface: Someone insists on having much more than control.
explanation.definitionFit: To dominate or rule a group is to have power over it, an idiom for control.

clue.text: Presentation of image less stuffy — almost plain

parts.note: PR, public relations, is the business of presenting an image

indicators.note: almost means the word for less stuffy is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: less stuffy means more airy, airier

explanation.surface: Image management that is a bit less stuffy is almost plain.
explanation.definitionFit: A prairie is a wide grassy plain, especially in North America.

clue.text: Sweat-covered man in middle of field finding shamrock?

indicators.note: Sweat-covered means the word for sweat wraps round the next piece

parts.note: to sweat is to toil, work hard
the referee stands in the middle of a football field, REF for short

explanation.surface: A sweaty referee in the centre of the pitch comes across a shamrock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweat-covered' looks like a description of the man, but it is the container signal; the question mark is there because a shamrock is only one kind of trefoil.
explanation.definitionFit: A shamrock is an example of a three-leaved clover, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Confirm demise of vessel after shelling

indicators.note: shelling means the outer letters, the shell, of the word for a ship's demise are stripped off

parts.note: a ship's end is its sinking

explanation.surface: Verify that a ship went down after being bombarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shelling' suggests gunfire sinking the ship, but it removes the first and last letters (S and G).
explanation.definitionFit: To go over pencil with pen is to finalise or confirm an arrangement, an idiom for making it definite.

clue.text: Random opium use not ultimately causing rash

indicators.note: random says the letters are jumbled in no set order
ultimately points to the final letter of the word not

explanation.surface: Taking opium haphazardly brings on a skin rash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rash' looks like a skin complaint, but it is the adjective meaning hasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe acting hastily without thought, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Quickly giving compere stick if introductions mixed up

indicators.note: introductions are first letters, so the opening letters of the two words are swapped

parts.note: a compere is a host
to stick is to paste

explanation.surface: Swiftly handing the presenter a stick if the introductions go wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introductions' looks like a compere's job, but it means the initial letters of HOST and PASTE, which swap.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means with great speed, originally of letters sent by fast post.

clue.text: Dolphins enjoy poking elderly relative affectionately

indicators.note: poking means one word is pushed into the middle of the other

parts.note: gramps is an affectionate name for a grandfather
to enjoy something, such as a privilege, is to have the use of it

explanation.surface: Dolphins like nudging Grandad fondly.
explanation.definitionFit: Grampus is the name of Risso's dolphin and loosely of other dolphin-like cetaceans, plural here.

clue.text: One who digs dirt concealed by a doctor

indicators.note: concealed by means the word for dirt is hidden inside the other letters

parts.note: mire is mud, dirt

explanation.surface: A man digging in dirt is hidden by a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' looks like excavating, but it is slang for likes.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig someone is slang for liking them, so a person who likes or appreciates is a fan.

clue.text: Swan interacting with mouse? New for a bird!

parts.note: a pen is a female swan
a GUI, graphical user interface, is what you interact with using a computer mouse

explanation.surface: A swan meeting a mouse, and swapped for a new bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mouse' looks like the animal, but it is the computer mouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The penguin is a flightless seabird of the southern hemisphere.

clue.text: Some knocked back tea — one guzzled port

indicators.note: knocked back says the hidden letters are read backwards
Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone downed tea, and another person gulped down port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' and 'guzzled' paint drinking, but 'knocked back' turns round the letters taken from 'tea one guzzled'.
explanation.definitionFit: Genoa is a major Italian seaport on the Ligurian coast, so it is a port city.

clue.text: Dance music in Lent is too much

indicators.note: in means the word for excessive sits inside the past tense

parts.note: lent, past tense of lend, is close to gave
OTT, over the top, means too much

explanation.surface: Dance music during Lent is excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lent' looks like the season of fasting, but it is the past tense of lend.
explanation.definitionFit: A gavotte is an old French dance, and also the music written for it.

clue.text: Rat seen moving extremely close

indicators.note: moving means the letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: A rat was seen scurrying very near.
explanation.definitionFit: Extremely close is the superlative of near, the closest of all.

clue.text: Jumbo the setter's set mostly to trap people

indicators.note: to trap means the earlier letters close round the word for people

parts.note: the setter refers to themself, the setter is = I'm

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word set is dropped

parts.note: people are men

explanation.surface: The setter is set on catching people with an elephant called Jumbo.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumbo as an adjective means very large, a synonym of huge or vast.

clue.text: German I note raised boy

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means the letters are read upwards, bottom to top

parts.note: I is one, and ein is German for one
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A German says 'I note' about raising a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' is the Roman numeral one, which in German is EIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie is a boy's name, short for Ernest.

clue.text: Husband welcome, since brave

parts.note: ave is a Latin greeting, hail or welcome
ago means since, in the past

explanation.surface: A husband is welcomed, since he was courageous.
explanation.definitionFit: A have-a-go hero is a bystander bold enough to tackle a criminal, so the adjective means plucky.

clue.text: Sailor who Roman knight would make legendary king

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
qui is Latin, the Roman tongue, for who
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A sailor asks which Roman knight would make a legendary king.
explanation.walkthrough: TARQUIN is Tarquinius Superbus, the semi-legendary last king of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarquin the Proud is the last of Rome's kings in its early, part-mythical history.

clue.text: Defiant remark: it follows comforting one

parts.note: so means therefore, it follows
the word said in 'there, there' to soothe someone is a comforting word

explanation.surface: A defiant retort comes after a comforting one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it follows' looks like a placement instruction but is a synonym for SO; 'comforting one' is the word repeated to console someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a cheeky declaration of triumph or defiance, said after getting one's way.

clue.text: Young stand-in priest, purged of sin, insincere fellow

indicators.note: purged of means the letters of the next word are cleared out of insincere

parts.note: taken as written
a gent is a gentleman, a fellow

explanation.surface: A youthful substitute priest, cleansed of sin, is a false fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purged of sin' reads as absolution, but it removes S, I, N from 'insincere', leaving INCERE.
explanation.definitionFit: George IV ruled as stand-in for his father George III while still a prince, a regent younger than the king he replaced.
